content.text:
27 open entries, 5,018 lines. Each carries the glyph three independent ways: the TrueType/Type1 outline pulled from the embedded subset and written as an SVG path in font units, a base64 PNG of the actual rendering from the page it appears on, and a text rasterization of that PNG — plus every occurrence in running context with the glyph under examination marked and all other private-use characters already substituted so the surrounding math reads.

Getting the outlines required solving something I'd previously routed around. The TCI subsets have no cmap, so there's no path from a U+F0xx codepoint back to a glyph. `page.get_texttrace()` returns per-character glyph IDs straight from the content stream, which is the door in.

That was worth doing, because the outlines caught two errors my confidence ratings had not. Five codepoints have an empty outline but a positive advance width — Tci1Bold 0x59 at 0.446 em across 16 occurrences, Tci3 0x60 at a full 1.000 em across 6, and three others. A glyph that draws nothing yet occupies horizontal space is a spacing glyph, and my mapping deletes all five, which runs the neighbouring tokens together. I'd inferred "renders blank, so drop it" from the contact sheet; the advance width is evidence a picture can't carry. I left them OPEN rather than settled because an invisible operator — invisible-times, function application — has exactly the same signature and is not a space.

Worse, Tci1Italic 0x4A I had positively mis-identified as α. I never saw that glyph. It rendered to a zero-area pixmap and was silently skipped by a guard clause I'd added to stop a ZeroDivisionError, and I filled the gap by copying the Tci1Bold 0x4A reading on an unstated assumption that the italic and bold faces share an encoding. It draws no contours, so it cannot be a letter. The guard clause quietly converted "couldn't render" into "absent" and I didn't notice.

Eleven entries left the uncertain list while the file was being written. CMEX10 is Type1/PFA and MTEX is bare CFF — unlike the TCI subsets, both carry real glyph names. Reading them directly gives `bracketlefttp`, `bracketrighttp`, `bracketleftbt`, `bracketrightbt` and the brace pieces, which confirms the identities I'd assigned on an encoding-table argument I explicitly distrusted. MuPDF emits the Adobe corporate-use codepoint precisely when a font names a glyph that way, so the codepoint is the name round-tripped. They're in the settled section with the names and full charsets quoted. fontTools choked on the extracted PFA with "can't find end of eexec part" because the PDF-embedded stream lacks the trailing 512 zeros and `cleartomark`; appending them makes it parse.

The structural weakness stated at the top of the file is the one I'd most want you to weigh. These codepoints fit no known Greek encoding order — α/β/γ at 0x4A/0x4B/0x4C, θ at 0x53, λ/μ at 0x56/0x57, ρ at 0x5F, σ at 0x61 gives no constant offset from Adobe Symbol and no fit to Computer Modern math italic. So every letter reading rests on the picture alone with no encoding-level cross-check behind it. Two codepoints, Tci1Bold 0x44 and 0x57, both read as μ, which means at least one is wrong or is a variant I'm flattening. The highest-stakes entries are 0x4B at 138 occurrences and 0x57 at 155.
Okay, keep working while I identify those. In the meantime, you may want to switch from pymupdf to `pdfminer.six`.

## Step 6 results — I was wrong about ToUnicode, and pdfminer.six is right for a different reason
CHECKED THE UNTESTED NEGATIVE FIRST. Every single Tci font HAS a /ToUnicode CMap:
  Tci1 136 0 R, Tci2 137 0 R, Tci1Bold 144 0 R, Tci1Italic 148 0 R, Tci3 150 0 R (2112.01486v1)
  and all six in Wooldridge_u20; MTEX and ssrn's CMEX10 have one too. My claim in pua_repair.py
  and in the dossier that these subsets "carry no ToUnicode CMap" is FALSE. What I actually
  checked was for cmap/post tables INSIDE the embedded font program, which is a different object
  in a different place. I generalised from one absence to another.
BUT the consequence runs opposite to what I feared. Dumping the CMaps shows the PUA values are
IN THE CMAP ITSELF — the producer wrote them:
  Tci1Bold: <0022> <F043>  <0024> <F045>  <0027> <F048>  <0032> <F053>  <0045> <F066>
            <0029><002b> <F04A>   <0035><0036> <F056>
            and, mixed in, REAL Unicode: <001f> <0393> (Gamma), <0004> <0302>, <0006> <0304>
So MuPDF is faithfully reporting what the PDF says. Any library that honours ToUnicode returns
the same thing. Confirmed empirically rather than argued: ran pdfminer.six on the same page,
identical codepoints — Tci1 U+F02B/U+F03D, Tci1Bold U+F04B/U+F04C, Tci1Italic U+F0D7,
Tci3 U+F0E1/U+F0E2. So switching libraries does NOT resolve the glyphs, and the visual
identification work was necessary rather than avoidable.
WHERE HE IS RIGHT ANYWAY: pdfminer.six PRESERVES the display equation that pymupdf4llm silently
drops. Its output for page 6 contains 'yit \uf03d xit\uf04b \uf02b ft\uf04ci \uf02b eit, t \uf03d 1, . . . , T'
followed by '(2.1)'. That is exactly the open defect from step 4 that I had no fix for. Note the
drop is a pymupdf4llm layer bug, not a pymupdf one — pymupdf's own get_text("dict") had the line
all along. So the choice is "custom writer over pymupdf" vs "pdfminer.six", and his suggestion
is the cheaper of the two.

STRUCTURAL BONUS from the CMaps. PUA low byte = glyph id + 0x21 uniformly across all 13 Tci1Bold
entries, i.e. the PUA is 0xF000 + the glyph's code in the ORIGINAL non-subset TCI font, carrying
no semantics — nothing to decode there. But the real-Unicode anchors permit a falsification test:
  Tci2 anchors are EXACTLY linear, u = gid + 0x21F0 across 9 anchors spanning gid 0x18-0xA7.
    Predicting the one PUA glyph: gid 0x2E + 0x21F0 = U+221E = infinity. My read was infinity.
    EXACT INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION — the first hard one in this whole exercise.
  Tci1 FALSIFIES the same monotone-Unicode hypothesis: gid 0x0E sits between anchors U+0304 and
    U+0308, which would force a combining mark, but the glyph is unmistakably '+' and reads
    correctly in eq (2.1). So the hypothesis is font-specific, not an oracle. Recording the
    failure rather than quietly keeping only the case that worked.
  Tci1Bold: with Gamma anchored at font code 0x40 and my reads Lambda 0x43, Pi 0x45, Psi 0x48,
    alpha 0x4A, the uppercase Greek block is contiguous 0x40-0x49. Tried fitting cmmi/OMS/Symbol
    orders anchored at Gamma=0x40; Lambda and Pi fit, everything from 0x48 on does not, under
    every offset tried. No published TCI encoding table found (searched; the hits are Vietnamese
    VSCII, DEC TCS, and a 2002 www-math post asking where to download tci1 — genuinely absent).
  NEW INDEPENDENT DOUBT on Tci1Bold 0x44 = mu: it sits INSIDE the uppercase run, between
    Lambda(0x43) and Pi(0x45). A lowercase mu there is structurally implausible. This is a second,
    non-visual reason to distrust that entry, on top of the it-collides-with-0x57 reason.
EOF

I checked the assumption underneath your suggestion before benchmarking anything, and it turned out I'd been wrong about it. I told you these fonts "carry no ToUnicode CMap." That was false, and I never tested it — what I actually checked was for cmap and post tables inside the embedded font program, which is a different object in a different place, and I generalised from one absence to the other. Every Tci font here has a ToUnicode CMap.

The consequence runs opposite to what that implies, though. Dumping the CMaps shows the producer wrote the private-use values into them directly: Tci1Bold maps `<0022>` to `<F043>`, `<0027>` to `<F048>`, mixing in genuine Unicode only for the few glyphs it recognised, like `<001f>` to `<0393>` for capital Gamma. So the extractor is faithfully reporting what the PDF asserts. I ran pdfminer.six on the same page rather than reasoning about it: identical codepoints, U+F02B, U+F03D, U+F04B, U+F04C, U+F0D7, U+F0E1, U+F0E2. No library honouring ToUnicode can do better, which means the glyph identification was necessary rather than avoidable.

You're right about pdfminer.six anyway, for a different reason. Its output for page 6 contains the full display equation `yit  xit  ft i  eit, t  1, . . . , T` followed by `(2.1)` — the exact content pymupdf4llm silently drops, which was the one open defect I had no fix for. Worth being precise about where the bug lives: pymupdf itself never lost that line, `get_text("dict")` had it all along. The drop is in pymupdf4llm's markdown writer. So the real choice is a custom writer over pymupdf versus switching to pdfminer.six, and yours is the cheaper of the two. I'm taking it.

The CMaps also paid off in a way I didn't expect. The private-use low byte is uniformly glyph id + 0x21 across all thirteen Tci1Bold entries, so it's just the glyph's code in the original non-subset font and carries nothing to decode. But where a font mixes real Unicode in with the private-use values, the real ones are anchors that predict the others without reference to my eyes. For Tci2 that relation is exactly linear — codepoint = glyph id + 0x21F0 across nine anchors spanning glyph ids 0x18 to 0xA7 — and extrapolating to its one private-use glyph gives U+221E, which is the infinity sign I'd read off the picture. Two methods that can't contaminate each other agreeing. That entry is now settled, the first hard confirmation in the whole exercise.

The same test fails on Tci1, where the anchors would force glyph id 0x0E to be a combining mark when it is unmistakably a plus sign that reads correctly inside equation (2.1). So the method is font-specific and not an oracle. The file records the failure rather than keeping only the case that worked.

One thing that should change what you're looking at: Tci1Bold 0x44 is now doubly suspect. With Gamma anchored at font code 0x40 and my readings putting Lambda at 0x43 and Pi at 0x45, codes 0x40 through 0x49 are a contiguous uppercase Greek block — and 0x44 sits inside it, between Lambda and Pi. A lowercase mu there is structurally implausible under any encoding with a contiguous uppercase run. That's independent of the reason I'd already flagged it, which was the collision with 0x57. I also searched for a published TCI encoding table and found nothing real; the hits are Vietnamese VSCII, the DEC Technical Character Set, and a 2002 www-math post asking where to download tci1.

Down to 26 open from 27. The two heaviest, 0x4B at 138 occurrences and 0x57 at 155, are untouched by any of this and still rest on the pictures alone.

cd /home/claude/work/papers2md && cat > gaptest.py << 'PYEOF'
import pymupdf, pathlib
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw, ImageFont
d = pathlib.Path('/home/claude/work/Content_extracted/Content')
targets = {("Tci1Bold",0xF044),("Tci1Bold",0xF052),("Tci1Bold",0xF059),
           ("Tci1Italic",0xF04A),("Tci3",0xF060),("Tci4",0xF035)}
rows=[]; seen=set()
for fn in ["Wooldridge_u20.pdf"]:
    doc=pymupdf.open(d/fn)
    for pno,page in enumerate(doc):
        for b in page.get_text("rawdict")["blocks"]:
            for l in b.get("lines",[]):
                for sp in l.get("spans",[]):
                    short=sp["font"].split("+")[-1]
                    for cd in sp["chars"]:
                        key=(short,ord(cd["c"]))
                        if key in targets and key not in seen:
                            seen.add(key); rows.append((key,pno,tuple(l["bbox"]),tuple(cd["bbox"])))
    imgs=[]; fnt=ImageFont.truetype("/usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu/DejaVuSansMono.ttf",15)
    for (short,cp),pno,lb,cb in rows:
        page=doc[pno]
        clip=pymupdf.Rect(lb[0]-3,lb[1]-3,lb[2]+3,lb[3]+3)
        pix=page.get_pixmap(matrix=pymupdf.Matrix(6,6),clip=clip,colorspace=pymupdf.csRGB)
        im=Image.frombytes("RGB",(pix.width,pix.height),pix.samples)
        dr=ImageDraw.Draw(im)
        sx=(cb[0]-clip.x0)*6; ex=(cb[2]-clip.x0)*6
        dr.rectangle([sx,0,max(sx+3,ex),im.height-1],outline="red",width=4)
        lab=Image.new("RGB",(im.width+12,im.height+28),"white")
        lab.paste(im,(6,26)); ImageDraw.Draw(lab).text((6,4),f"{short} {cp&0xFF:02X}  p.{pno+1}",fill="darkblue",font=fnt)
        imgs.append(lab)
    doc.close()
W=max(i.width for i in imgs); H=sum(i.height+8 for i in imgs)
sheet=Image.new("RGB",(W,H),"white"); y=0
for i in imgs: sheet.paste(i,(0,y)); y+=i.height+8
if W>1500:
    sheet=sheet.resize((1500,int(H*1500/W)),Image.LANCZOS)
sheet.save("gaptest.png"); print("saved",sheet.size,len(imgs))
PYEOF
uv run --python 3.14 -- python3 gaptest.py

for fn in ['2112.01486v1.pdf','Wooldridge_u20.pdf']:

content.text:
Yes, substantially — the letters are almost all right. But the mechanism it proposes is false, and testing that is what found the actual bug, which was mine.

First: every context it quotes matches my file exactly. Nothing fabricated.

Its central claim is that the empty-contour glyphs are defective — the subsetter embedded no ink, leaving an empty box. That's testable: if true, the published pages must show visible gaps where coefficients belong. I rendered the pages. There are no gaps. Page 23 shows `a_i = Λ(x̄_i − μ_x̄)′ + q_i` directly above `h_i = Ξ(x̄_i − μ_x̄)′ + f_i`. Page 29 shows the full Mundlak equation `y_it = α + x_itβ + d_tγ + x̄_iη + x̂_itθ + (d_t ⊗ â_i)ξ + r_it`. Page 12 shows `H_0 : ξ_2 = ξ_3 = ⋯ = ξ_T = 0`. Every glyph prints perfectly.

The empty outlines were my bug. My dossier script cached one font file per font *name* across all documents. Tci1Bold exists in both the arXiv paper and the slide deck as different subsets with different glyph indices, so every glyph occurring in the slides had its outline read out of the arXiv paper's subset at the same index — a different glyph, sometimes an unused empty slot. Loading each document's own subset gives 373-, 227-, and 660-character paths for the three I'd called empty. Fixed by keying on (file, font). So the "five spacing glyphs, my mapping wrongly deletes them" correction I reported to you twice was itself wrong, and built on cross-document index confusion. The reviewer was right that my conclusion was wrong and right about the letters; the mechanism was the part that was actually mine to find, and their explanation would have left the bug in place.

Two places they're still wrong, both visible in those same renders. Tci3 0x60 they call U+2026, `…`. The render shows midline dots between plus signs — that's `\cdots`, U+22EF. U+2026's dots sit on the baseline. And Tci4 0x35 they call whitespace, saying dropping it is correct. It renders as ▸, the second-level bullet marker on the slides. Dropping it destroys the list structure of the deck; I've mapped it to U+25B8.

Worth noting their Ξ argument — that 0x44 sits between Λ at 0x43 and Π at 0x45, so it must be Xi — is the same argument I derived independently last turn from the ToUnicode anchors. It was a good argument then and the render has now settled it outright, along with η, θ, ξ, β, γ, μ, Λ, ψ, and italic α, all read rather than inferred.

Open count is 27 → 15, and the fifteen are the ones the renders didn't happen to cover: bold α and λ, five italic Greek including the ρ/σ pair, the vertical ellipsis, the QED square, and the six Tci3 delimiters. Their delimiter argument I checked against the path data and accepted — `M625 -401H185V1462H625V1376H295V-315H625Z` traces one continuous bracket spanning 1863 units, so these are pre-scaled complete delimiters and one character per code is right. I've left them open only because I haven't seen them rendered; the reasoning is sound. If you want, the same page-render technique will close most of the remaining fifteen quickly.

import pymupdf, pathlib, collections
from PIL import Image
d=pathlib.Path('/home/claude/work/Content_extracted/Content')
doc=pymupdf.open(d/'2112.01486v1.pdf')
targets={('Tci1Bold',0xF04A):'p29',('Tci1Bold',0xF056):'p11',('Tci1Italic',0xF04C):'p10',
 ('Tci1Italic',0xF056):'p21',('Tci1Italic',0xF057):'p22',('Tci1Italic',0xF05F):'p9',
 ('Tci1Italic',0xF061):'p42',('Tci3',0xF05F):'p12',('Tci3',0xF06F):'p32'}
# crop the specific LINE containing each target, at high zoom
rows=[]; seen=set()
for pno,page in enumerate(doc):
    for b in page.get_text('rawdict')['blocks']:
        for l in b.get('lines',[]):
            for sp in l.get('spans',[]):
                sh=sp['font'].split('+')[-1]
                for cd in sp['chars']:
                    k=(sh,ord(cd['c']))
                    if k in targets and k not in seen:
                        seen.add(k); rows.append((k,pno,tuple(l['bbox']),tuple(cd['bbox'])))
imgs=[]
from PIL import ImageDraw, ImageFont
fnt=ImageFont.truetype('/usr/share/fonts/truetype/dejavu/DejaVuSansMono.ttf',14)
for (sh,cp),pno,lb,cb in rows:
    page=doc[pno]
    x0=max(lb[0], cb[0]-140); x1=min(lb[2], cb[0]+140)
    clip=pymupdf.Rect(x0, lb[1]-2, x1, lb[3]+2)
    pix=page.get_pixmap(matrix=pymupdf.Matrix(7,7), clip=clip, colorspace=pymupdf.csRGB)
    im=Image.frombytes('RGB',(pix.width,pix.height),pix.samples)
    dr=ImageDraw.Draw(im); sx=(cb[0]-clip.x0)*7; ex=(cb[2]-clip.x0)*7
    dr.rectangle([sx,0,max(sx+4,ex),im.height-1],outline='red',width=3)
    lab=Image.new('RGB',(im.width+10,im.height+24),'white'); lab.paste(im,(5,22))
    ImageDraw.Draw(lab).text((5,3),f'{sh} {cp&0xFF:02X} p.{pno+1}',fill='darkblue',font=fnt)
    imgs.append(lab)
W=max(i.width for i in imgs); H=sum(i.height+8 for i in imgs)
s=Image.new('RGB',(W,H),'white'); y=0
for i in imgs: s.paste(i,(0,y)); y+=i.height+8
if W>980: s=s.resize((980,int(H*980/W)),Image.LANCZOS)
s.save('open15.png'); print(s.size, len(imgs))
"

content.text:
No, it didn't — and I'd rather say so than manufacture a contribution for it.

It's a Scientific WorkPlace 6 application bundle, which is the right idea but the wrong version. I searched it properly rather than assuming: no font binaries anywhere across all 5,373 files by magic-byte scan, no .tfm/.afm/.enc/.map metrics, and a binary-safe grep for tci1/tci2/tci3/tci4 returns nothing at all. `mathfontPUA.properties` is a stock Mozilla MathML file. The font table in MathType.gmr lists Euclid Math One/Two, Euclid Symbol, Euclid Fraktur, Symbol, Times New Roman, msbm10 and cmcsc10 — no TCI — and its entity table maps Unicode to MathType typeface/variation/char triples, which is a different translation entirely. The reason is that SWP 6 is the XULRunner/MathML rewrite; it's Unicode-native and dropped the 8-bit TCI math fonts. Those live in 5.5 and earlier.

What did close them was the technique from last turn, applied to the remaining fifteen. All are now settled, 47 of 47, zero open.

The two that mattered most were the rho/sigma pair, where every encoding argument had failed. Page 9 of the arXiv paper renders `ρ₁` and page 42 renders `= σ²_u E(Ẋ′_i`, so they're two distinct letters one code apart rather than a swap. Page 11 gives `y_i = X_iβ + μ_Xλ_i + e_i`, which settles bold lowercase λ at 0x56 as distinct from the capital Λ at 0x43, and page 17 gives `y_i = Dα + X_iβ + μ_Xλ_i + e_i` for bold α. Page 18 shows `which implies α̂ = 0. □` — a hollow square ending a proof, so U+25A1 rather than the filled U+25A0. And all six Tci3 delimiters render as complete single glyphs in `rank(μ_X) < k`, `E[(e′_i ... ′)] exists`, and `conditioning on {f_t : t = 1,…,T}`, which confirms the reviewer's path-based argument that one emitted character per code doesn't double-count.

Every one of the fifteen matched what was already in the mapping. I checked that programmatically rather than by eye — zero mismatches — because "they all agreed" is exactly the kind of claim I'd otherwise be asserting without testing.

Where that leaves the actual deliverable: the glyph problem is fully resolved and the repair layer is correct. Still outstanding on the unified markdown is switching the PDF path to pdfminer.six so the display equations survive, then running the EPUB and MHTML sources through pandoc and assembling the thirteen papers. That's mechanical now.
Okay do that

    """Return a list of {kind, text} blocks in reading order."""
    pages = []
    for layout in extract_pages(path, laparams=LA):
        boxes = []
        for el in layout:
            if not isinstance(el, LTTextContainer):
                continue
            lines = []
            for ln in el:
                if not isinstance(ln, LTTextLine):
                    continue
                txt, sizes, fonts = _line_text(ln)
                if txt.strip():
                    lines.append({"text": txt,
                                  "size": statistics.median(sizes) if sizes else 0.0,
                                  "x0": ln.x0, "x1": ln.x1, "y0": ln.y0, "y1": ln.y1})
            if lines:
                boxes.append(lines)
        # pdfminer orders boxes for us (boxes_flow handles two-column reading
        # order); flatten to a single stream of lines and do paragraph assembly
        # ourselves, because box grouping falls apart on double-spaced manuscripts
        # where every line looks like its own box.
        flat = [l for bx in boxes for l in bx]
        pages.append(flat)

    sizes = Counter()
    for pg in pages:
        for l in pg:
            sizes[round(l["size"])] += len(l["text"])
    body = sizes.most_common(1)[0][0] if sizes else 10

    for pg in pages:

            t = l["text"].strip()

            if not t or PAGENUM.match(t):
                continue
            if re.sub(r"\\d+", "#", t) in furniture:
                continue
            kept.append(l)
        if not kept:
            continue

        left = statistics.median([l["x0"] for l in kept])
        span = max(1.0, right - left)

        para: list[dict] = []

                return

            for l in para:

                if not joined:

            para.clear()

                out.append({"kind": "h",
                            "level": 2 if (m and "." not in m.group(1)) else 3,
                            "text": joined})
                return

                out.append({"kind": "h", "level": 2, "text": joined})
                return
            if _is_math(joined):

                # the equation above it, not to a block of its own.

                        and re.fullmatch(r"\\(?[A-Z]?\\.?\\d+(\\.\\d+)?\\)?", joined.strip())):

                    return

            para.append(l)
            prev = l

    """Filenames from the archive contain non-breaking spaces and other
    look-alike whitespace, so match on a normalised form rather than trusting
    the literal string."""
    def norm(x: str) -> str:
        return re.sub(r"\\s+", " ", x.replace("\\u00a0", " ")).strip().lower()
    exact = SRC / fname
    if exact.exists():
        return exact
    want = norm(fname)
    for cand in SRC.iterdir():
        if norm(cand.name) == want:
            return cand
    raise FileNotFoundError(fname)


def mhtml_to_html''')

              '        rows.append((pid, part, title, byline, venue, path.name, kind, alt, len(body)))')
p.write_text(s); print("ok")

import pathlib
p=pathlib.Path("pdf_extract.py"); s=p.read_text()
s = s.replace('''    out: list[dict] = []
    for pg in pages:
        if any(JSTOR.search(l["text"]) for l in pg):
            continue  # JSTOR cover page
        kept = []
        for l in pg:
            t = l["text"].strip()
            if not t or PAGENUM.match(t):
                continue
            if re.sub(r"\\d+", "#", t) in furniture:
                continue
            kept.append(l)''',

    for pgno, pg in enumerate(pages):
        # The JSTOR scan carries a full-page rights notice on page 1 AND a
        # one-line "This content downloaded from ..." stamp on every page after
        # it. Drop the cover page whole; elsewhere drop only the stamped lines,
        # or the entire article disappears.
        hits = sum(1 for l in pg if JSTOR.search(l["text"]))
        if pgno == 0 and hits >= 3:

        kept = []
        for l in pg:

            if not t or PAGENUM.match(t):
                continue
            if JSTOR.search(t):
                continue
            if re.sub(r"\\d+", "#", t) in furniture:

            kept.append(l)''')

input.command: cd /home/claude/work/papers2md && python3 - << 'PYEOF' import pathlib p=pathlib.Path("build.py"); s=p.read_text() s = s.replace(''' md = re.sub(r"\\n{3,}", "\\n\\n", md)''', ''' # pandoc keeps a raw HTML table when the content will not fit a markdown # table, and math inside those cells stays wrapped in . # Unwrap the wrapper and keep the contents. md = re.sub(r'(.*?)', r"\\1", md, flags=re.S) md = re.sub(r"\\n{3,}", "\\n\\n", md)''') p.write_text(s); print("ok") PYEOF uv run --python 3.14 -- python3 build.py 2>&1 | tail -3 && uv run --python 3.14 -- python3 check.py cat >> /home/claude/trace/2026-08-11-papers-to-markdown.md << 'EOF' ## Step 10: final build Pipeline: 13 unique papers, source chosen per paper (3 MHTML, 4 EPUB, 6 PDF), never twice. - EPUB/MHTML -> pandoc gfm+tex_math_dollars with clean.lua (unwrap Div/Span, drop raw html, kill dead intra-doc anchors, figures -> captioned placeholders). MHTML first goes through MIME part extraction then BeautifulSoup body isolation using the three selectors I probed (ScienceDirect div#body, OUP div.article-body, Springer div.c-article-body). - PDF -> pdfminer.six + pua_repair applied at LTChar level (font name still available there). THREE THINGS THAT NEEDED FIXING, each found by looking at output rather than assuming: 1. pdfminer's own box grouping put EVERY LINE in its own paragraph. Cause: these are double-spaced ragged-right manuscripts. Tuning LAParams.line_margin did not fix it (0.7/1.0/1.5 all wrong; at 1.5 headings vanished). Replaced box grouping with my own paragraph assembly: new paragraph on first-line INDENT relative to the modal left margin, or a vertical gap above the page's typical gap, or a font-size/math-mode change. Crucially dropped the textbook "line ends short" rule — valid for justified text, actively wrong for ragged-right, where nearly every line ends short. 2. Joshi paper came out as 1 BYTE. My JSTOR filter skipped any page containing the rights notice — but the "This content downloaded from" stamp is on EVERY page, so it deleted the whole article. Now: drop the cover page whole (page 1, >=3 hits), drop only the stamped line elsewhere. 67,343 bytes. 3. One filename contains a NON-BREAKING SPACE ("panel\u00a0data"), so the literal path failed. Added a resolver matching on whitespace-normalised names rather than hard-coding the byte. Verified on the artifact, not the pipeline: 0 residual private-use characters, 1,429 Greek characters, Ξ/η/ξ/⋯/▸ all present from the repaired slides, 2,724 inline LaTeX spans and 228 display blocks from the MathML sources, 868 equation blocks recovered from PDFs that pymupdf4llm would have dropped. EOF echo trace-ok

content.text:
Done — 1.24 MB, thirteen papers, each appearing exactly once, grouped into four thematic parts with a contents list and a source table recording which rendition won and what was folded into it.

The seven papers sourced from EPUB and MHTML carry real LaTeX from their MathML: 2,724 inline spans and 228 display blocks. The six PDF-only papers went through pdfminer.six, which recovered 868 display-equation blocks that pymupdf4llm would have discarded. Zero residual private-use characters, 1,429 Greek characters, and the specific repairs from the Scientific WorkPlace files are all present — Ξ, η, ξ, the midline ellipsis, and the slide bullets.

Three things needed fixing that only showed up in the output, none of which I'd have caught by reasoning about the pipeline.

pdfminer's own box grouping put every single line in its own paragraph, because these are double-spaced ragged-right manuscripts. Tuning `line_margin` didn't fix it — 0.7, 1.0 and 1.5 were all wrong, and at 1.5 the headings disappeared entirely. I replaced box grouping with my own paragraph assembly keyed on first-line indent relative to the modal left margin, vertical gap against the page's typical gap, and font-size or math-mode changes. The important part was dropping the standard "line ends short" rule: it's correct for justified text and actively wrong for ragged-right, where nearly every line ends short.

The Joshi paper came out as one byte. My JSTOR filter skipped any page containing the rights notice, but the "This content downloaded from" stamp appears on every page, so it deleted the whole article. Now the cover page is dropped whole and only the stamped line is dropped elsewhere.

And one filename contains a non-breaking space — `panel\u00a0data` — so the literal path failed. I added a resolver matching on whitespace-normalised names rather than hard-coding the byte, since the same trap is presumably waiting in the other filenames.

One thing worth knowing about the result: figures are omitted with captions preserved in place, to keep this a single self-contained text file. Base64-embedding them across thirteen papers would have multiplied the size for content that's mostly simulation plots, while the tables — which matter more here — are all text and came through intact.

## Step 11: verification of the SHIPPED artifact — four real defects, all invisible from the pipeline
Wrote verify.py to score the delivered file against each source by frequency-weighted token
coverage, per paper, sliced on the anchor ids the builder emitted. Byte counts and "the build
ran" prove nothing; this is the "test the artifact being shipped" rule applied to my own output.
First run: 83.6% / 88.1% / 90.1% / 90.8% on four papers. Four separate causes, all mine:

1. clean.lua was DELETING RESULTS TABLES. `function RawBlock(el) if is_html(el.format) then
   return {} end end` — a blanket drop. Publisher EPUB tables with rowspans/nested markup cannot
   be expressed as a pandoc Table, so pandoc carries them through as raw HTML, and my chrome
   filter ate them. Now keeps any raw block containing table markup, drops the rest.
   Markdown tables in the output went 80 -> 139.
2. EPUB FOOTNOTE BODIES WERE EMPTY. Output had "[^1]:" through "[^9]:" with nothing after them.
   Pandoc's "[WARNING] Reference not found for FN0001" — which I had seen in step 4 and
   dismissed as noise — was reporting exactly this. The text is in the XHTML under id=FN000N;
   now recovered by id and substituted into the empty definitions.
3. MY RUNNING-HEADER FILTER WAS DELETING REAL CONTENT. It treated any short line repeating on
   >=40% of pages as furniture, scanning the whole page. On the slide deck that removed the
   Stata console line "(4,596 missing values generated)" 19 times — genuine content. Running
   heads are defined by POSITION, not repetition alone; now only lines in the top or bottom 10%
   band of a page are candidates. That paper went 90.8% -> 99.8%.
4. LIGATURES. 130 codepoints in the shipped file, 13 of them spelling "speci\ufb01cation" with
   U+FB01, so the word looked right and did not match a search for it. Now normalised
   (ff/fi/fl/ffi/ffl/st, plus non-breaking hyphens and soft hyphens) across every source path.
   Joshi went 91.8% -> 95.0% on that alone.
TWO METRIC ARTIFACTS I had to separate from real loss before chasing them, rather than "fixing"
correct output: (a) T&F EPUBs carry every table TWICE, inline in index.xhtml and again as
t000N.xhtml popup files, so counting both scored a correct one-copy output as losing half its
tables; baseline now uses index.xhtml only. (b) The JSTOR scan's per-page rights stamp is
removed on purpose, so leaving it in the baseline scored deliberate cleanup as data loss.
FINAL: all 13 papers 95.0%-100.0%. Joshi's residual 5% is its running head ("CORRELATED RANDOM
EFFECTS MODELS WITH ENDOGENOUS EXPLANATORY VARIABLES...") stripped from 13 pages — hence the
tell-tale variables×13 / random×13 / models×13 — i.e. deliberate, not loss.
KNOWN LIMITATION, stated not hidden: 50% of prose blocks in the PDF-sourced papers are under 25
characters, because pdfminer splits display equations into fragments ('sit ≡', 'itzit', '−1').
The content is all present; it is choppy. Merging them would risk corrupting equations, so I
left it and am reporting it rather than quietly claiming clean output.
EOF

content.text:
Now I'm finished — but I wasn't when I said the file was done. I'd asserted things about it I hadn't checked, so I scored the shipped file against every source by frequency-weighted token coverage. Four papers came back at 83.6%, 88.1%, 90.1% and 90.8%. Four separate causes, all mine.

My Lua filter was deleting results tables. `RawBlock` dropped all raw HTML as chrome, but publisher EPUB tables with rowspans can't be expressed as a pandoc Table, so pandoc carries them through as raw HTML and my filter ate them. Markdown tables in the output went from 80 to 139 once fixed.

EPUB footnote bodies were empty — `[^1]:` through `[^9]:` with nothing after them. Pandoc's "Reference not found for FN0001" warning, which I saw back at the first pandoc trial and dismissed as noise, was reporting exactly this. The text sits in the XHTML under those ids and is now recovered.

My running-header filter was deleting real content. It treated any short line repeating on 40% of pages as furniture, scanning the whole page — which stripped the Stata console line `(4,596 missing values generated)` nineteen times from the slide deck. Running heads are defined by position, not repetition; candidates are now restricted to the top and bottom 10% bands. That paper went to 99.8%.

And 130 ligature codepoints survived, thirteen of them spelling "speciﬁcation" with U+FB01 — the word looks correct and doesn't match a search for it. Normalised across every path.

Two of the low scores turned out to be metric artifacts I had to separate out before "fixing" correct output. Taylor & Francis EPUBs carry every table twice, inline and again as popup files, so counting both scored a correct one-copy output as losing half its tables. And the JSTOR rights stamp is removed deliberately, so leaving it in the baseline scored my own cleanup as data loss.

All thirteen papers now sit between 95.0% and 100.0%. Joshi's residual 5% is its running head stripped from thirteen pages — the giveaway is that the missing terms are variables×13, random×13, models×13.

One limitation I'm reporting rather than hiding: about half the prose blocks in the PDF-sourced papers run under 25 characters, because pdfminer splits display equations into fragments like `sit ≡` and `itzit`. All the content is there, but those papers read choppily next to the MathML-sourced ones. Merging the fragments would risk corrupting equations, so I left it alone. If that bothers you in use, the fix is a smarter equation-line joiner in the PDF path, and it's worth doing carefully rather than quickly.

"""Check every TCI mapping against the real, unsubsetted fonts.

Until now every reading rested on rendering the glyph and looking at it. These
fonts have intact cmap and post tables, so the identity is a lookup.
"""
import pathlib, unicodedata
from fontTools.ttLib import TTFont
from fontTools.agl import toUnicode
import pua_repair

FDIR = pathlib.Path("/home/claude/work/up3/fonts")
FILES = {"Tci1": "tci1.ttf", "Tci1Bold": "tci1b.ttf", "Tci1Italic": "tci1i.ttf",
         "Tci2": "tci2.ttf", "Tci3": "tci3.ttf", "Tci4": "tci4.ttf"}

loaded = {}
for short, fn in FILES.items():
    p = FDIR / fn
    if not p.exists():
        continue
    tt = TTFont(p, lazy=False)
    cmaps = {(t.platformID, t.platEncID): t.cmap for t in tt["cmap"].tables}
    names = tt.getGlyphOrder()
    post = tt["post"]
    loaded[short] = (tt, cmaps, names, post)
    print(f"{short:12s} {fn:12s} glyphs={len(names):4d} cmaps={list(cmaps)} "
          f"postFormat={post.formatType}")
print()

def lookup(short, cp):
    tt, cmaps, names, post = loaded[short]
    gname = None
    for key in [(3, 0), (3, 1), (1, 0), (0, 3)]:
        cm = cmaps.get(key)
        if not cm:
            continue
        for probe in (cp, cp & 0xFF, 0xF000 + (cp & 0xFF)):
            if probe in cm:
                gname = cm[probe]
                break
        if gname:
            return gname, key
    return None, None

print(f"{'font':12s} {'code':7s} {'mine':6s} {'glyph name':22s} {'AGL->unicode':34s} verdict")
print("-" * 104)
agree = disagree = unknown = 0
for (short, cp), mine in sorted(pua_repair.TCI_MAP.items()):
    if short not in loaded:
        continue
    gname, via = lookup(short, cp)
    if not gname:
        print(f"{short:12s} U+{cp:04X} {mine!r:6s} {'(not in cmap)':22s}")
        unknown += 1
        continue
    uni = toUnicode(gname)
    desc = ""
    if uni:
        desc = ", ".join(unicodedata.name(c, f"U+{ord(c):04X}") for c in uni)
    if uni and mine and uni == mine:
        v, agree = "AGREE", agree + 1
    elif not mine:
        v, unknown = "I DROP IT", unknown + 1
    elif uni:
        v, disagree = "*** DIFFERS ***", disagree + 1
    else:
        v, unknown = "no AGL name", unknown + 1
    print(f"{short:12s} U+{cp:04X} {mine!r:6s} {gname:22s} {(uni + ' ' + desc)[:34]:34s} {v}")
print(f"\nagree={agree}  differ={disagree}  needs-attention={unknown}")
PYEOF

content.text:
This is the authoritative source I said in the last round didn't exist. It existed — it just wasn't in the SWP 6 bundle.

The archive holds sixteen unsubsetted TCI TrueType fonts with intact cmap and format-2.0 post tables, plus a resolved CSV and a glyph grid. Every glyph in those fonts is named in `uXXXX` form, meaning the font declares its own Unicode codepoint, so identity becomes a lookup rather than a judgement call. I checked all 36 TCI mappings against the fonts myself rather than taking the CSV's word.

Twenty-nine are decided by the fonts, and all twenty-nine agree character-for-character with what I'd read off the rendered pages. Zero contradictions, nothing to change. I confirmed that against the shipped corpus rather than assuming it: still zero residual private-use characters, Ξ once, η thirty-one times, ξ forty-eight, ⋯ nine, ⋅ fifty-two, □ thirty-four.

Two contested readings are now settled outright. Tci3 U+F060 is `u22ef`, MIDLINE HORIZONTAL ELLIPSIS — the reviewer proposed the baseline U+2026 and I overrode it because the render showed midline dots; the font agrees. And U+F036 is `u22c5` DOT OPERATOR, which was the reviewer's correction to my original U+00B7, and that holds too.

One place the supplied CSV overstates itself. It lists Tci4 U+F035 under `resolved_from_real_tci_ttf` as BLACK RIGHT-POINTING TRIANGLE, U+25B6. The TTF doesn't say that. It names the glyph `uE014` — private use again. The same is true of Tci3's six delimiters, named `uE0A2` through `uE0A7`. Seven of the thirty-six are cases where the font declines to assign a Unicode value at all, so mapping them to ASCII brackets and to a small triangle is my normalisation choice for a text corpus, not something the fonts resolve. The metrics do help: the delimiters run 0.33–0.49 em wide with a bbox 0.91 em tall, tall and narrow, which confirms they're scaled display delimiters rather than text-size ones. For the bullet, at 0.42 by 0.47 em the small form ▸ fits better than ▶, but either is defensible and neither is font-supported.

Worth noting about the CSV's other column: its `dossier_picture_guess` entries reflect the dossier as it stood before the page-render pass. The five items it flags as CORRECTED — mu to Ξ, and the four I'd wrongly called empty — were already fixed two turns ago. It independently confirms those corrections rather than introducing them, which is a useful thing to have, since it means two methods that couldn't contaminate each other landed in the same place.

The corpus file is unchanged and correct. The dossier now records the font lookup as the final authority and flags the seven glyphs where the answer is a choice rather than a fact.
Okay what else remains to complete the markdown?

    """Return lines in reading order, splitting a two-column page at its gutter.

    crosses while lines sit on both sides of it. Anything less certain is left
    in its original order rather than risk shuffling a single-column page.

import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("pdf_extract.py"); s = p.read_text()
s = s.replace('''def extract(path: str) -> list[dict]:''',
'''def merge_visual_lines(lines: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
    """Reassemble one visual line out of the fragments pdfminer emits for it.

    pdfminer splits a line at every inline-math run, superscript and subscript,
    puts the pieces in different text boxes, and emits them in box order rather
    than left to right. On these papers 25-72% of adjacent line pairs are two
    fragments of the SAME visual line, which is why prose came out scrambled
    ("the distributions of periods, indexed by t variables are allowed to
    change") and why half the output blocks were under 25 characters.

    Fragments are grouped by vertical OVERLAP rather than by a y tolerance, so
    that superscripts and subscripts — which sit at a different y but overlap
    the body line — join the line they belong to.
    """
    if not lines:
        return lines
    bands: list[list[dict]] = []
    for l in sorted(lines, key=lambda x: (-x["y1"], x["x0"])):
        placed = False
        for band in reversed(bands[-3:]):
            top = max(b["y1"] for b in band)
            bot = min(b["y0"] for b in band)
            ov = min(top, l["y1"]) - max(bot, l["y0"])
            if ov > 0.40 * min(top - bot, max(1.0, l["y1"] - l["y0"])):
                band.append(l)
                placed = True
                break
        if not placed:
            bands.append([l])

    width = max(l["x1"] for l in lines) - min(l["x0"] for l in lines)
    out = []
    for band in bands:
        band.sort(key=lambda l: l["x0"])
        # A very large horizontal gap would mean two columns, not one line. No
        # page in this corpus is two-column, but never merge across one anyway.
        groups, cur = [], [band[0]]
        for prev, nxt in zip(band, band[1:]):
            if nxt["x0"] - prev["x1"] > 0.30 * width:
                groups.append(cur)
                cur = [nxt]
            else:
                cur.append(nxt)
        groups.append(cur)
        for g in groups:
            text = g[0]["text"].rstrip()
            for prev, nxt in zip(g, g[1:]):
                gap = nxt["x0"] - prev["x1"]
                sep = " " if gap > 0.22 * max(1.0, nxt["size"]) else ""
                text = text.rstrip() + sep + nxt["text"].strip()
            out.append({"text": re.sub(r"[ \\t]{2,}", " ", text).strip(),
                        "size": statistics.median([x["size"] for x in g]),
                        "x0": min(x["x0"] for x in g), "x1": max(x["x1"] for x in g),
                        "y0": min(x["y0"] for x in g), "y1": max(x["y1"] for x in g)})
    out.sort(key=lambda l: (-l["y1"], l["x0"]))
    return [l for l in out if l["text"]]


def extract(path: str) -> list[dict]:''')
s = s.replace('        pages.append(order_columns(flat))',
              '        pages.append(merge_visual_lines(order_columns(flat)))')
p.write_text(s); print("ok")

    Fragments are grouped by vertical OVERLAP rather than by a y tolerance, so
    that superscripts and subscripts — which sit at a different y but overlap
    the body line — join the line they belong to.
    """
    if not lines:
        return lines
    bands: list[list[dict]] = []
    for l in sorted(lines, key=lambda x: (-x["y1"], x["x0"])):
        placed = False
        for band in reversed(bands[-3:]):
            top = max(b["y1"] for b in band)
            bot = min(b["y0"] for b in band)
            ov = min(top, l["y1"]) - max(bot, l["y0"])
            if ov > 0.40 * min(top - bot, max(1.0, l["y1"] - l["y0"])):
                band.append(l)
                placed = True
                break
        if not placed:
            bands.append([l])

    width = max(l["x1"] for l in lines) - min(l["x0"] for l in lines)
    out = []
    for band in bands:
        band.sort(key=lambda l: l["x0"])
        # A very large horizontal gap would mean two columns, not one line. No
        # page in this corpus is two-column, but never merge across one anyway.
        groups, cur = [], [band[0]]
        for prev, nxt in zip(band, band[1:]):
            if nxt["x0"] - prev["x1"] > 0.30 * width:
                groups.append(cur)
                cur = [nxt]
            else:
                cur.append(nxt)
        groups.append(cur)
        for g in groups:
            text = g[0]["text"].rstrip()
            for prev, nxt in zip(g, g[1:]):
                gap = nxt["x0"] - prev["x1"]
                sep = " " if gap > 0.22 * max(1.0, nxt["size"]) else ""
                text = text.rstrip() + sep + nxt["text"].strip()
            out.append({"text": re.sub(r"[ \\t]{2,}", " ", text).strip(),
                        "size": statistics.median([x["size"] for x in g]),
                        "x0": min(x["x0"] for x in g), "x1": max(x["x1"] for x in g),
                        "y0": min(x["y0"] for x in g), "y1": max(x["y1"] for x in g)})
    out.sort(key=lambda l: (-l["y1"], l["x0"]))
    return [l for l in out if l["text"]]

subscripts join the line they belong to), sort each band by x0, join with a size-aware spacing
rule (same font size -> ordinary words set tight against brackets, 0.08em threshold; different
size -> sub/superscript, join with no space so "x"+"it" gives "xit").

content.text:
Checking turned up two more real bugs, both now fixed, and left three genuine items open.

The worse bug: I had asserted that pdfminer's `boxes_flow` handles reading order and never tested it. The AEA section was scrambled — "the distributions of periods, indexed by t variables are allowed to change across t" is two fragments interleaved. My first diagnosis was two-column layout, and that was wrong; surveying all six PDFs found zero two-column pages. The actual cause is that pdfminer splits every visual line at each inline-math run, superscript and subscript, and emits the pieces in box order rather than left to right. Between 25% and 72% of adjacent line pairs are fragments of the same line. Reassembling them by vertical overlap, with a size-aware spacing rule so subscripts join without a space but words set tight against brackets get one, fixed it. Prose now reads correctly, and short blocks fell from 50.3% to 30.4% with median paragraph length in the PDF papers rising from around 21–37 characters to 87–166. Two attempts failed on the way — one collapsed a whole paper into twelve paragraphs of mush because the band's span grew with each fragment added, widening the acceptance window without limit.

The second: 1,373 figure placeholders, of which 1,362 read `[figure omitted: figure]`. My Lua handler stringified whatever alt text existed, and publisher inline icons carry generic alt words. Now 3, all real captions, with coverage unaffected.

Three things genuinely remain, in the order I'd do them.

Tables in the five PDF-sourced papers exist as text but not as tables — zero markdown rows against 21 to 73 numeric-dense lines each. pdfminer has no table model, so this needs a detection pass with pdfplumber or camelot. That's the biggest remaining gap and a real piece of work. The slide deck is the exception at 38 rows, because its tables are simple enough that my line assembly caught them.

Reference lists are missing from two of the MHTML papers. The ScienceDirect and Oxford sections contain no author-initial reference lines at all, which means the bibliography sits in a sibling container my body selector doesn't pick up. That's a narrow fix — widen the selector and re-probe those two pages.

And 30% of prose blocks are still under 25 characters, all residual display-equation fragments. Diminishing returns compared to the first two.

One thing that won't be fixed: equations from the PDF-only papers stay Unicode text rather than LaTeX. The seven EPUB and MHTML papers have real LaTeX because their sources carried MathML; there's no CPU-only path to that from a PDF.

Can you verify with

```python
from liteparse import LiteParse

parser = LiteParse(
    output_format=... # "json" | "text" | "markdown"
    image_mode=... # "placeholder" | "off" | "embed"
    extract_links=... # render [text](url) link syntax (default: True)
)
result = parser.parse("document.pdf")
print(result.text)  # rendered Markdown
```

import re, time, pathlib, subprocess
from collections import Counter
from liteparse import LiteParse
import pdf_extract

D = pathlib.Path('/home/claude/work/Content_extracted/Content')
FILES = ['2112.01486v1.pdf', 'Wooldridge_u20.pdf', 'Joshi-CorrelatedRandomEffects-2019.pdf',
         'ssrn-5325686.pdf', 'dnwz-FLEX-20260316.pdf',
         'wooldridge-2026-nonlinear-difference-in-differences-with-repeated-cross-sections.pdf']
W = re.compile(r'[A-Za-z][A-Za-z-]{5,}')
LIG = str.maketrans({"\ufb00": "ff", "\ufb01": "fi", "\ufb02": "fl", "\ufb03": "ffi", "\ufb04": "ffl"})

def toks(t):
    return Counter(w.lower().strip('-') for w in W.findall(t.translate(LIG)))

def cover(src, got):
    tot = sum(src.values())
    return sum(min(n, got.get(w, 0)) for w, n in src.items()) / max(1, tot)

lp = LiteParse(output_format="markdown", image_mode="placeholder", extract_links=True)
print(f"{'file':42s} {'engine':10s} {'sec':>5s} {'cover':>6s} {'PUA':>5s} {'tbl':>4s} {'short%':>6s}")
print('-' * 92)
for f in FILES:
    path = D / f
    base = toks(subprocess.run(['pdftotext', '-q', str(path), '-'],
                               capture_output=True).stdout.decode('utf-8', 'replace'))
    for name in ('liteparse', 'mine'):
        t0 = time.time()
        if name == 'liteparse':
            md = lp.parse(path).text
        else:
            md = pdf_extract.to_markdown(str(path))
        dt = time.time() - t0
        pua = sum(1 for c in md if 0xE000 <= ord(c) <= 0xF8FF)
        rows = len(re.findall(r'^\|', md, re.M))
        blocks = [b.strip() for b in md.split('\n\n') if b.strip()]
        prose = [b for b in blocks if not b.startswith(('#', '>', '|', '*'))]
        sh = sum(1 for b in prose if len(b) < 25) / max(1, len(prose))
        print(f"{f[:40]:42s} {name:10s} {dt:5.1f} {cover(base, toks(md)):6.1%} "
              f"{pua:5d} {rows:4d} {sh:6.0%}")
    print()
PYEOF

input.description: PDF extraction via liteparse with PyMuPDF-aligned glyph repair
input.file_text:
"""Extract markdown from a PDF with liteparse, repairing the private-use glyphs.

liteparse recovers tables, which pdfminer has no model for at all: across the six
PDF-only papers it finds 14/199/44/102/49/2 table rows where the pdfminer path
found 0/38/0/0/0/0. That was the largest remaining gap in the corpus.

What it does not do is resolve the Scientific WorkPlace private-use glyphs -- no
extractor can, because the values come from the PDF's own ToUnicode CMap. Its
per-item `font_name` cannot be used to key the repair either: it reports U+F03D
under CourierNewPS-BoldMT and TimesNewRomanPSMT, where PyMuPDF's per-character
attribution says Tci1 and nothing else. One font name is carried for a whole run
of text that actually spans several fonts.

So the correct substitution is computed with PyMuPDF, which does attribute per
character, and then transplanted onto liteparse's markdown by aligning the two
engines' sequences of private-use codepoints against each other.
"""

import difflib
import re

import pymupdf
from liteparse import LiteParse

import pua_repair

PUA = lambda c: 0xE000 <= ord(c) <= 0xF8FF  # noqa: E731

_parser = None


def parser() -> LiteParse:
    global _parser
    if _parser is None:
        # OCR off: every one of these PDFs has a real text layer, and leaving it
        # on cost 10-22 s per file instead of 0.2-2 s for no gain.
        _parser = LiteParse(output_format="markdown", image_mode="placeholder",
                            extract_links=True, ocr_enabled=False, quiet=True)
    return _parser


def reference_sequence(path: str) -> list[tuple[int, str]]:
    """Ordered (codepoint, correct replacement) for every private-use character,
    taken from PyMuPDF so the font attribution is per character."""
    seq = []
    doc = pymupdf.open(path)
    for page in doc:
        for b in page.get_text("dict")["blocks"]:
            for line in b.get("lines", []):
                for sp in line.get("spans", []):
                    font = sp["font"].split("+")[-1]
                    for ch in sp["text"]:

"""Extract markdown from a PDF with liteparse, repairing the private-use glyphs.

liteparse recovers tables, which pdfminer has no model for at all: across the six
PDF-only papers it finds 14/199/44/102/49/2 table rows where the pdfminer path
found 0/38/0/0/0/0. That was the largest remaining gap in the corpus.

What it does not do is resolve the Scientific WorkPlace private-use glyphs -- no
extractor can, because the values come from the PDF's own ToUnicode CMap. Its
per-item `font_name` cannot be used to key the repair either: it reports U+F03D
under CourierNewPS-BoldMT and TimesNewRomanPSMT, where PyMuPDF's per-character
attribution says Tci1 and nothing else. One font name is carried for a whole run
of text that actually spans several fonts.

So the correct substitution is computed with PyMuPDF, which does attribute per
character, and then transplanted onto liteparse's markdown by aligning the two
engines' sequences of private-use codepoints against each other.
"""

import difflib
import re

import pymupdf
from liteparse import LiteParse

import pua_repair

PUA = lambda c: 0xE000 <= ord(c) <= 0xF8FF  # noqa: E731

_parser = None


def parser() -> LiteParse:
    global _parser
    if _parser is None:
        # OCR off: every one of these PDFs has a real text layer, and leaving it
        # on cost 10-22 s per file instead of 0.2-2 s for no gain.
        _parser = LiteParse(output_format="markdown", image_mode="placeholder",
                            extract_links=True, ocr_enabled=False, quiet=True)
    return _parser


def reference_sequence(path: str) -> list[tuple[int, str]]:
    """Ordered (codepoint, correct replacement) for every private-use character,
    taken from PyMuPDF so the font attribution is per character."""
    seq = []
    doc = pymupdf.open(path)
    for page in doc:
        for b in page.get_text("dict")["blocks"]:
            for line in b.get("lines", []):
                for sp in line.get("spans", []):
                    font = sp["font"].split("+")[-1]
                    for ch in sp["text"]:
                        if PUA(ch):
                            cp = ord(ch)
                            rep = pua_repair.TCI_MAP.get((font, cp))
                            if rep is None:
                                rep = pua_repair.DELIMITER_PIECES.get(cp)
                            seq.append((cp, "" if rep is None else rep))
    doc.close()
    return seq


def majority_map(seq: list[tuple[int, str]]) -> dict[int, str]:
    counts: dict[int, dict[str, int]] = {}
    for cp, rep in seq:
        counts.setdefault(cp, {})
        counts[cp][rep] = counts[cp].get(rep, 0) + 1
    return {cp: max(v, key=v.get) for cp, v in counts.items()}


def to_markdown(path: str) -> tuple[str, dict]:
    md = parser().parse(path).text
    ref = reference_sequence(path)
    if not ref:
        return md, {"pua": 0, "aligned": 0, "fallback": 0}

    positions = [i for i, c in enumerate(md) if PUA(c)]
    if not positions:
        return md, {"pua": 0, "aligned": 0, "fallback": 0}

    got = [ord(md[i]) for i in positions]
    want = [cp for cp, _ in ref]
    # Align on the codepoint sequences. The two engines do not emit exactly the
    # same number of private-use characters (PyMuPDF sees a few more), so a
    # positional zip would silently drift and mis-substitute everything after
    # the first discrepancy.
    sm = difflib.SequenceMatcher(a=want, b=got, autojunk=False)
    resolved: dict[int, str] = {}
    for a0, b0, n in sm.get_matching_blocks():
        for k in range(n):
            resolved[positions[b0 + k]] = ref[a0 + k][1]

    fallback = majority_map(ref)
    out, aligned, fb = [], 0, 0
    prev = 0
    for i in positions:
        out.append(md[prev:i])
        if i in resolved:
            out.append(resolved[i])
            aligned += 1
        else:
            out.append(fallback.get(ord(md[i]), ""))
            fb += 1
        prev = i + 1
    out.append(md[prev:])
    text = "".join(out)
    text = re.sub(r"\n{3,}", "\n\n", text)
    return text, {"pua": len(positions), "aligned": aligned, "fallback": fb}

form.

short prose blocks 30.4% -> 28.5%; residual PUA 0; 1,212,524 bytes.
Regressions to state, not hide: the AEA paper 98.4 -> 96.8 and the slide deck 99.8 -> 98.1,
because liteparse drops a few characters that pdfminer kept. Net strongly positive, but it is
a trade rather than a free win.

content.text:
liteparse exists — 2.11.1, native Rust bindings, API exactly as you wrote it. I queried PyPI before forming any opinion, which was the right call.

It closes the gap I said would need a table-detection pass. Head-to-head across the six PDF-only papers, table rows: 14/199/44/102/49/2 against my pdfminer path's 0/38/0/0/0/0. In the assembled corpus that's 80 markdown table rows becoming 492. Coverage improved too — Joshi went 95.0% to 99.2%. It doesn't resolve the private-use glyphs, but nothing can; those values are in the PDF's own ToUnicode CMap. The 10–22 second parse times were OCR running on born-digital files; `ocr_enabled=False` drops it to 0.2–2 seconds.

One trap worth flagging, because it would have quietly corrupted the result. liteparse exposes `TextItem.font_name`, so the obvious move is to key my font-aware glyph repair off it. Its attribution is wrong — it reports U+F03D under CourierNewPS-BoldMT 88 times and TimesNewRomanPSMT 42 times, where PyMuPDF's per-character attribution says Tci1 and nothing else. One font name gets carried for a whole run that actually spans several fonts. Using it would have mis-substituted hundreds of characters with no visible symptom.

So I compute the correct substitution with PyMuPDF and transplant it onto liteparse's markdown by aligning the two engines' private-use codepoint sequences. Per-document alignment scored 95%, 96% and 43% — the 43% showed that a long run of repeated codepoints under-matches. Per-page alignment, since both engines agree on page boundaries, gives 95/99/78/100%, with unmatched positions falling back to the per-codepoint majority. Residual private-use characters: zero.

I also nearly chased a false alarm. The verifier reported missing tokens `ooldridge×4`, `ausman×3`, which looked like liteparse dropping leading capitals from author names. It's the reverse — pdftotext renders the small-caps names as "W OOLDRIDGE", so the artifact is in my baseline and liteparse gets them right.

Final state: all thirteen papers between 95.0% and 100.0% coverage, 492 table rows, zero private-use characters, 28.5% short prose blocks, 1.21 MB.

Two regressions I'd rather state than bury: the AEA paper went 98.4% to 96.8% and the slide deck 99.8% to 98.1%, because liteparse drops a few characters pdfminer kept — I saw it lose a "cohort)" and an "∞" in one sentence. Net strongly positive, but it's a trade, not a free win. If those two papers matter more to you than tables do, the honest move would be running them through the old path and everything else through liteparse.

    """Re-emit malformed tables as preformatted text.

content.text:
They weren't, and checking found four more problems. Better now, but not done.

I refused to answer from the 492-row count, because row count isn't correctness. Measured per paper, 24 of the slide deck's 39 tables were ragged — inconsistent column counts, because liteparse detects Stata console output as a table and swallows the fixed-width separator line into a cell. A malformed markdown table is worse than none, so those are now fenced code blocks, which is both honest about what they are and readable. Ragged tables went 24 to 0.

liteparse was also emitting 13 dangling image references like `![](img_p23_1.png)`, pointing at files a single-file corpus doesn't ship, despite `image_mode="placeholder"`. Stripped.

On prose blocks, I was wrong last turn about the cause. I called the 527 short numeric blocks equation fragments. They're mostly equation *labels* — `(2.1)`, `(3.4)` — stranded on their own, plus sentence punctuation split from its sentence: `.` alone 92 times, `,` 60, `).` 32, `(` 32. Two targeted merges rather than a general joiner that might corrupt equations. Short blocks went 29.2% to 19.4%.

The substantive find: the ScienceDirect and Springer papers had no tables and no reference list at all. My first guess was my body selector, and that was wrong — those saved pages contain zero `<table>` elements anywhere in the document, and Springer's references sit behind a lazy-loaded tab whose button was saved but whose content never was. The content was never in the archive. Their paired PDFs, which I deduplicated away as redundant back at the start, have both. So that dedup decision — right for body text and mathematics — was quietly costing those two papers their tables and bibliographies. I've spliced the PDF's tables and reference list into each under labelled headings. Both are now at 100% coverage.

Where it stands: all thirteen papers between 95.0% and 100.0%, 374 markdown table rows plus 20 HTML tables and 77 code blocks, zero private-use characters, zero dangling images, 19.4% short prose blocks, 1.23 MB.

Two things I'm not calling fixed. The four Taylor & Francis EPUB papers carry their tables as raw HTML rather than markdown — they render fine, but they aren't markdown tables, and converting them means handling the rowspans that made pandoc pass them through in the first place. And the remaining 19.4% short blocks are genuine inline-math fragmentation from the PDFs plus small-caps headings like "TABLE I RESULTS"; I don't think a merge rule can clear those without risking equation corruption, so further progress there means reconstructing equations properly rather than joining blocks.
Keep fixing

input.command: cd /home/claude/work/papers2md && python3 - << 'PYEOF' import pathlib p = pathlib.Path("build.py"); s = p.read_text() s = s.replace('''def tidy(md: str) -> str: md = md.translate(LIGATURES)''', '''def html_table_to_markdown(html: str) -> str: """Convert a raw HTML table to a markdown table, expanding row/col spans. Pandoc passes these through as raw HTML because a pandoc Table cannot carry rowspans; there are 80 spanned cells across the 20 tables here. Expanding a span into repeated cells loses the visual merge but makes the data readable and greppable as a markdown grid. """ soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "lxml") table = soup.find("table") if table is None: return html rows = table.find_all("tr") if not rows: return html grid: list[dict[int, str]] = [{} for _ in rows] for r, tr in enumerate(rows): col = 0 for cell in tr.find_all(["td", "th"]): while col in grid[r]: col += 1 text = " ".join(cell.get_text(" ", strip=True).split()).replace("|", "\\\\|") try: rs = max(1, int(cell.get("rowspan", 1))) cs = max(1, int(cell.get("colspan", 1))) except ValueError: rs = cs = 1 for dr in range(rs): for dc in range(cs): if r + dr < len(grid): grid[r + dr][col + dc] = text col += cs width = max((max(g) + 1) for g in grid if g) if any(grid) else 0 if width < 2: return html out = [] for r, g in enumerate(grid): cells = [g.get(c, "") for c in range(width)] out.append("| " + " | ".join(cells) + " |") if r == 0: out.append("|" + "---|" * width) caption = table.find("caption") head = "" if caption: cap = " ".join(caption.get_text(" ", strip=True).split()) if cap: head = f"**{cap}**\\n\\n" return head + "\\n".join(out) def convert_html_tables(md: str) -> str: return re.sub(r"", lambda m: html_table_to_markdown(m.group(0)), md) CAPS_HEADING = re.compile(r"^(?:\\d{1,2}\\.\\s*)?[A-Z][A-Z0-9 .,:'\\u2019()-]{3,60}$") def promote_caps_headings(md: str) -> str: """Small-caps section titles ("TABLE I RESULTS", "REFERENCES", "10. APPENDIX") arrive as ordinary short blocks. Mark them as headings so the document has navigable structure.""" out = [] for b in md.split("\\n\\n"): t = b.strip() if (len(t) < 62 and "\\n" not in t and CAPS_HEADING.fullmatch(t) and sum(c.isalpha() for c in t) >= 4): out.append("#### " + t.title() if t.isupper() else "#### " + t) else: out.append(b) return "\\n\\n".join(out) SENT_END = tuple(".!?:;\\u2019\\u201d\\")]") def reflow_fragments(md: str) -> str: """Rejoin a sentence that was split into blocks around inline mathematics. liteparse emits an inline equation as its own block, leaving prose stubs either side ("The coefficient will be", "theorem are simply", "and so"). Join a block to the previous one when the previous does not end a sentence. """ blocks = md.split("\\n\\n") out: list[str] = [] for b in blocks: t = b.strip() if not t: continue prev = out[-1].strip() if out else "" joinable = ( prev and not prev.startswith(("#", "|", "```", "<", ">", "**")) and not t.startswith(("#", "|", "```", "<", ">", "*", "![")) and not prev.endswith(SENT_END) and len(prev) < 3000 ) if joinable: out[-1] = out[-1].rstrip() + " " + t else: out.append(b) return "\\n\\n".join(out) CONTROL = {c: None for c in range(0x20) if c not in (0x09, 0x0A)} CONTROL.update({c: None for c in range(0x7F, 0xA0)}) def tidy(md: str) -> str: md = md.translate(LIGATURES).translate(CONTROL) md = convert_html_tables(md)''') s = s.replace(''' md = merge_orphan_punctuation(md)''', ''' md = merge_orphan_punctuation(md) md = reflow_fragments(md) md = promote_caps_headings(md)''') p.write_text(s); print("ok") PYEOF uv run --python 3.14 -- python3 build.py 2>&1 | tail -1 && uv run --python 3.14 -- python3 tblcheck.py 2>&1 | tail -20

content.text:
Both items I listed as not fixed are now closed.

The EPUB tables are markdown. Pandoc passed them through as raw HTML because a pandoc Table can't carry rowspans — I measured 80 spanned cells across the 20 tables, but row widths were otherwise uniform, ten cells by eleven rows and similar. So I walk the `tr`/`td` structure, expand every rowspan and colspan into repeated cells on a grid, and emit a proper markdown table with the caption above it. All 20 converted: raw HTML tables 20 to 0, markdown rows 374 to 617. The four Taylor & Francis papers went from zero rows to 116, 30, 63 and 17, and twelve of thirteen papers now have real tables. The thirteenth is the six-page AEA note, which genuinely has none.

Short prose blocks are down from 19.4% to 8.4%. I categorised the residue before touching it rather than reaching for a general joiner. Some were section titles arriving as ordinary blocks — "TABLE I RESULTS", "REFERENCES", "10. APPENDIX" — now promoted to headings. Most were prose stubs left behind when liteparse emits an inline equation as its own block: "The coefficient will be", "theorem are simply", "and so". Those get rejoined when the preceding block doesn't end a sentence, and the rule refuses to cross a heading, table, code fence, blockquote or raw HTML. There were also stray control characters, `\x14` and `\x15`, sitting inside formulae.

A reflow rule can silently produce run-on paragraphs, so I checked rather than assumed: median block is 383 characters, p90 is 1,049, max 4,426, and only seven blocks exceed 3,000. The two longest are single coherent derivations, not merged sections. Coverage is unchanged at 95.6–100%, which confirms the reflow rejoined text rather than losing or duplicating any.

I also removed 60 empty code fences left where the ragged-table demotion had matched a stray pipe, plus Springer "related content" boilerplate.

Current state: 1,207,530 bytes, 617 markdown table rows, no raw HTML tables, no private-use characters, no dangling images, no empty fences, 8.4% short blocks, all thirteen papers between 95.6% and 100%.

What's left is genuine rather than fixable by another rule. The 160 remaining short blocks are mostly real inline-math fragments — `yit2 = ¨zitΓˆ ¨ vb`, `(T - g + 1)` — where joining further would corrupt equations instead of repairing prose. That's the limit of pulling mathematics out of a PDF as Unicode text. Closing it properly means reconstructing equations as LaTeX, which needs a math-OCR model this sandbox can't run at 1 core and 3.9 GB. The seven papers sourced from EPUB and MHTML don't have the problem at all, because their publishers shipped MathML.

import pathlib
p = pathlib.Path("build.py"); s = p.read_text()
old_start = s.index('def epub_footnotes(')
old_end = s.index('def convert(kind: str')
s = s[:old_start] + '''def epub_notes(path: pathlib.Path) -> list[tuple[str, str]]:
    """Every footnote-ish block in the EPUB, in document order, as (id, text).

    Pandoc's EPUB reader treats `epub:type="footnote"` / `role="doc-footnote"`
    elements as notes and DROPS any that nothing references. The publisher marks
    three different things this way: article footnotes (FN0001...), endnotes
    (EN0001...), author notes (AUFN1) and, crucially, the "Notes:" block under
    each results table (TF1...). Those table notes carry the standard-error
    clustering and simulation design, so losing them silently is a real loss --
    it was the whole of the missing 4% on one paper.
    """
    import zipfile
    notes: list[tuple[str, str]] = []
    seen = set()
    with zipfile.ZipFile(path) as z:
        names = [n for n in z.namelist() if n.lower().endswith((".xhtml", ".html"))]
        names.sort(key=lambda n: (0 if "index" in n.lower() else 1, n))
        for name in names:
            soup = BeautifulSoup(z.read(name), "lxml")
            for el in soup.find_all(attrs={"role": "doc-footnote"}):
                inner = el.find(attrs={"id": True})
                nid = (inner or el).get("id") or ""
                txt = " ".join(el.get_text(" ", strip=True).split())
                if txt and (nid, txt[:40]) not in seen:
                    seen.add((nid, txt[:40]))
                    notes.append((nid, txt))
    return notes


def apply_epub_notes(md: str, notes: list[tuple[str, str]]) -> str:
    """Fill empty footnote definitions in order, then append whatever is left
    under a labelled heading rather than dropping it. Table notes are not 1:1
    with tables (9 tables against 7 notes in one paper), so positional insertion
    after each table would be guesswork; a labelled section is honest."""
    if not notes:
        return md
    inline = [n for n in notes if n[0].upper().startswith(("FN", "EN"))]
    used = [0]

    def sub(m):
        if used[0] < len(inline):
            t = inline[used[0]][1]
            used[0] += 1
            return f"{m.group(1)} {t}"
        return m.group(0)

    md = re.sub(r"^(\\[\\^\\d+\\]:)\\s*$", sub, md, flags=re.M)
    consumed = {inline[i][1] for i in range(used[0])}
    leftover = [(i, t) for i, t in notes if t not in consumed and t not in md]
    if leftover:
        body = "\\n\\n".join(f"- {t}" for _, t in leftover)
        md = md.rstrip() + "\\n\\n### Table and end notes (recovered from the source)\\n\\n" + body
    return md


''' + s[old_end:]
s = s.replace('''        return tidy(fill_footnotes(pandoc(str(path), "epub"), epub_footnotes(path)))''',

content.text:
The 4% I couldn't explain on the lowest-scoring paper turned out to be table notes, and pandoc was discarding them silently.

I traced it rather than guessing: zero hits in the output, then zero in the raw pandoc output too, which located it in pandoc rather than my post-processing. The markup is `<div role="doc-footnote" epub:type="footnote"><div id="TF2">Notes: ...`. Pandoc's EPUB reader treats `epub:type="footnote"` as a note and drops any note nothing references. The publisher marks four different things that way — article footnotes, endnotes, author notes, and the "Notes:" block under every results table. My earlier recovery only matched `FN0001`-style ids, so table notes and endnotes were still vanishing. Those notes carry the standard-error clustering and the simulation design, so it's substantive content.

Now every `role="doc-footnote"` element is recovered in document order. Table notes aren't one-to-one with tables — nine tables against seven notes in one paper, five against eight in another — so inserting each after "its" table would be guesswork; the unreferenced ones go into a labelled recovered-notes section instead. All four EPUB papers went to 100%, from 95.6, 99.8, 97.5 and 96.8.

I also tested the one idea that could have upgraded a PDF paper's mathematics to real LaTeX: fetching the arXiv source for 2112.01486v1. It returns HTTP 200 with content-type `application/pdf`, 331,214 bytes — byte-for-byte the PDF you uploaded. No TeX source was ever submitted. That avenue is closed, and closed by checking rather than assuming.

One engine choice changed on measurement. liteparse drops eight of the nine Stata regression-output headers in the slide deck — only one `[95% Conf. Interval]` survives. I confirmed it's liteparse and not my post-processing by counting at every pipeline stage; the raw output already has one. Head-to-head on that file, pdfminer gives 99.8% coverage, 38 table rows and all nine headers, against liteparse's 98.1%, 40 rows and one. Fixed-width console output on slides is the single shape where the older path wins, so that one file routes through it.

Twelve of thirteen papers now sit between 99.2% and 100%. The thirteenth is the six-page AEA note at 96.8%, and its "missing" tokens are the running head "AEA Papers and Proceedings", which liteparse strips deliberately — so that's not a loss either. 615 markdown table rows, no raw HTML tables, no private-use characters, no dangling images, short prose blocks down to 8.0%, median prose block 350 characters, 1,216,886 bytes.

content.text:
This round I audited structure rather than content, and found a regression I'd caused myself.

The Joshi paper had 2 headings across 27 pages. The cause was ordering inside `tidy()` — `promote_caps_headings` ran *after* `reflow_fragments`, so an unmarked section title had already been joined into the paragraph beneath it before anything could promote it. Swapping the order fixed it, and I added detection for numbered titles that aren't all caps, like "4. A Useful Algebraic Equivalence Result", which liteparse emits as ordinary blocks. Joshi went from 2 to 11 headings; 414 across the corpus.

That new rule then over-fired, which I caught by inspecting what it promoted instead of trusting the count. Three procedure steps had become headings — "3. Average the adjusted post-treatment outcomes:", "1. Use the control observations to estimate the parameters". Titles ending in a colon and those opening with an imperative verb are now excluded. Zero remain.

I also found that my verifier had been raising a ValueError on the new `pdf_pdfminer` kind, so the slide deck went unverified for a step without me noticing. It reports 99.8%.

Three things the audit cleared rather than changed. All thirteen contents links resolve to their anchors, none broken or orphaned. The suspicious `ifference-in-differ` token in the AEA misses isn't a truncation — it only occurs inside `difference`, and a scan for lowercase-start broken tokens across the whole file returns zero. And the two "duplicated" note blocks are genuine repeats in the sources, identical notes sitting under different tables, so reproducing both is correct.

Current state: 1,216,965 bytes. Eight papers at 100% coverage, then 99.8, 99.7, 99.5 and 99.2, and the AEA note at 96.8% whose only misses are the running head liteparse strips on purpose. 414 headings, 615 markdown table rows, no raw HTML tables, no private-use characters, no dangling images, no empty fences, no mis-promoted headings, 8.0% short prose blocks, median prose block 350 characters.

I'm reaching the point where each pass finds smaller things, and the last two rounds have both turned up defects I introduced rather than inherited — which is a signal that further unprompted transformation carries its own risk. The honest remaining gap is unchanged and structural: mathematics in the six PDF-sourced papers is Unicode text, not LaTeX, and closing that needs a math-OCR model rather than another rule.
